events.title: The September 11 attacks
events.description: Terrorist attacks kill thousands of people in the United States. Communities mourn and help those affected.

events.title: Microsoft and the US government propose a settlement
events.description: The agreement would restrict some business practices. Court review and other legal steps remain.

events.title: Euro cash enters everyday use
events.description: Twelve countries introduce euro notes and coins.

events.title: Columbia is lost
events.description: The space shuttle breaks apart during its return to Earth, killing its seven crew members.

what_happened_next.text:
Bonds led the seven choices. All three company shares lost heavily: Cisco lost more than three-quarters, while Microsoft and Amazon lost about half. The US basket also fell, but much less than those individual stocks. A useful technology and a promising business could still be disappointing investments at the price paid.

In November 2001, Microsoft and the US government proposed a settlement of their competition case. The legal story had moved forward, though review was still required.

The period included the September 11 attacks, the arrival of euro notes and coins, and the loss of the Columbia shuttle. These events belong to the history of the five years. They do not by themselves explain the exact return of a software company, retailer or equipment maker.

The company losses show why the price at the start matters. A business can sell something people need and still give shareholders a poor return. Paying for great expectations leaves room for disappointment. A broad US basket lost value too, but it spread the risk across many companies instead of concentrating it in these three. That reduced the loss here without preventing it altogether.

reflection.what_people_were_focused_on: Investors saw online books, internet broadcasting and networking equipment as signs of a changing economy. Taiwan’s election and scientific discoveries competed for attention.
reflection.what_actually_mattered: The price paid and the full five-year path mattered. Spreading money across many companies reduced dependence on these three badly hit shares.
reflection.what_faded_away: The number of people downloading a story did not reveal a software or networking company’s future return. Exciting new habits were not automatic stock-market gains.
reflection.what_nobody_knew: Nobody knew the size of the losses ahead. The internet’s importance did not make every share price reasonable or every company a winner.

hot_stock_outcomes.text: Cisco began this window near the height of internet-stock excitement. Customer orders then collapsed, leaving equipment and parts it could not sell as expected. In 2001, Cisco cut the recorded value of those unsold goods by $2.2 billion, helping create a large quarterly loss. Annual profit recovered to $4.4 billion in 2004, but that recovery could not undo the huge drop from the stock’s boom-time price.

The technology boom ended, but Microsoft’s software business kept earning money. Office and Windows Server helped annual sales reach $36.84 billion in June 2004. MSN also recorded its first profitable year, while legal settlements and a European fine added costs. Those business gains were not enough to support the much higher share price investors had paid near the boom’s peak.

Amazon’s shopping business improved even while its shares remained far below their boom-time price. In 2004, sales grew 31% to $6.92 billion and profit from operations reached $440 million. In February 2005, Amazon launched Prime, offering members fast shipping for an annual fee. These gains and new plans did not recover the stock’s high March 2000 starting price.
